sections.h1: Exterior and Outdoor Business Signs in New York City
sections.lead_html:
Your exterior sign is the first thing customers and visitors see.

Vision Graphics designs and makes exterior signs that NYC storefronts and buildings use, from channel letters and blade signs to building and monument signs, and manages installation through licensed partners.

We plan outdoor business signs around permits, building approval, and New York weather, so the sign you approve is the sign that goes up.

sections.h2: Exterior Signs We Design, Make and Install
sections.intro_html: Pick the sign that fits how people see your building. Our custom exterior signs and exterior business signs are grouped by location, and each page covers options, materials, and what to expect.

groups.label: Storefront Signs
groups.intro_html: Signs for the front of a shop, restaurant, or office. These outdoor commercial signs work at street level, day and night.

items.title: Channel Letter Signs
items.html: Individually built letters with LED lighting, front-lit or halo-lit, mounted straight to the facade. These lighted outdoor business signs read clearly after dark and suit most storefronts. Channel letter signs in NYC.

items.title: Storefront Signs
items.html: Fascia panels and lightboxes sized for your frontage. A storefront sign is your business's main name at street level. Storefront signs in NYC

items.title: Blade Signs
items.html: Projecting signs that catch walkers from both directions. Blade signs hang over the sidewalk, so projection and size rules matter.

items.title: Dimensional Letter Signs
items.html: Raised letters in metal or acrylic with clean shadow lines. They suit professional offices and storefronts that want a refined, architectural look. Dimensional letter signs in NYC

items.title: Cabinet Signs
items.html: Lit boxes with a replaceable face. Cabinet signs suit buildings and landlords that allow them, and some historic districts do not.

groups.label: Building and Property Signs
groups.intro_html: Signs that name a building, a campus, or a property. Outdoor building signs and exterior building signs keep tenants and visitors oriented.

items.title: Building Signs
items.html: Identification for the whole building. Building signs carry the name, address, and tenant marks on a wall or canopy.

items.title: Monument Signs
items.html: Freestanding signs at an entrance. Monument signs suit business parks and campuses, especially in the outer boroughs.

items.title: Pylon Signs
items.html: Tall signs on one or two poles. Pylon signs suit roadside sites, and zoning often limits them on dense blocks.

items.title: Post and Panel Signs
items.html: Simple signs on posts for small sites. Post and panel signs suit offices, clinics, and lots with a setback.

groups.label: Window Graphics
groups.intro_html: Vinyl lettering, frosted film, and full-window displays. Window graphics carry a message at street level and can be updated easily.

sections.intro_html: New York City regulates exterior signs. Your sign may need several approvals, and the list depends on its size, lighting, mounting, and location.

items.title: Sign Permit
items.html: Most exterior signs may require a DOB sign permit. A non-illuminated sign of six square feet or less generally does not, but zoning still applies.

items.title: Electrical and Illuminated Sign Permits
items.html: A lit sign may require a separate electrical permit filed by a licensed electrician. A lit sign that extends beyond the building line may also require an annual illuminated sign permit.

items.title: Zoning
items.html: Your zoning district sets how large a sign can be and how it may be lit. We check the rules for your address before the design is final.

items.title: Landmarks and Historic Districts
items.html: Signs on landmarked buildings or in historic districts may require written approval from the Landmarks Preservation Commission. Those rules often favor non-lit or halo-lit lettering.

items.title: Landlord and Building Approval
items.html: Your landlord or building management may require approval of the sign drawings, and some leases set their own sign rules. Send your lease's sign guidelines early.

items.title: Licensed Installation
items.html: A licensed sign hanger may be required to install or supervise the work, with exemptions for small signs. Our licensed installation partners handle the filing and installation, and our team prepares the drawings. See how sign installation in NYC works.

items.title: Existing Signs and Local Law 15 of 2026
items.html:
NYC has temporary protections through February 8, 2028, for certain accessory signs in place by February 9, 2025, and DOB encourages owners to bring existing signs into compliance before then.

The protections do not make a noncompliant sign lawful, and they do not cover a new replacement sign. Ask our team about your sign.

sections.h2: Ready to Plan Your Exterior Sign?
sections.html: Send photos of your facade and your address, and tell us which sign you have in mind. Our team will come back with questions, a drawing, and a quote.

sections.intro_html: New York weather is hard on exterior signs: sun, freeze-thaw cycles, wind-driven rain, and road salt.

items.title: Materials
items.html: Powder-coated aluminum holds up well outdoors. UV-stable faces resist fading, and stainless hardware resists rust.

items.title: Lighting
items.html: LED modules in outdoor business signs should be rated for outdoor use. Sealed enclosures keep moisture out of lit signs, and a licensed electrician makes the final connection.

items.title: Maintenance
items.html: Plan a periodic check. Clean the faces, check the mounting hardware, and replace failed lighting before it becomes a safety issue.

sections.after_html: A common rule of thumb for size is about one inch of letter height per 10 feet of viewing distance. We confirm the size on a drawing of your facade.

sections.h2: How an Exterior Sign Project Works
steps: Survey: Send photos of your facade or book a survey. We check the wall, height, and access.
Design: You approve a drawing showing size, color, lighting, and placement.
Permits: We prepare the drawings and coordinate the licensed filer for the permits your sign may require.
Fabrication: We make the sign, check it against the drawing, and ship it.
Installation: Licensed partners install on your schedule, with after-hours options. See how sign installation in NYC works.

sections.intro_html: Exterior signs follow the same basics for each business: a clear brand, the right sign type, and a building that approves it. See signs for Manhattan and Brooklyn businesses.

items.q: Do I need a permit for an exterior sign in NYC?
items.a_html: Usually yes. Most exterior signs may require a DOB sign permit, and a lit sign may also need an electrical permit and, if it extends beyond the building line, an annual illuminated sign permit. A non-illuminated sign of six square feet or less generally does not, but zoning still applies. We prepare the drawings and coordinate the licensed filer.

Lit signs read after dark and suit storefronts open in the evening, but they may need electrical and illuminated sign permits. Non-lit signs involve fewer permits and less upkeep, and landmark districts often favor non-lit or halo-lit lettering. Tell us your address and hours, and we will recommend one.

Most exterior signs take three to five weeks to fabricate and ship, plus DOB permit review and, where it applies, landmark review. Permits often set the schedule, so we start them early. Tell us your target date, and we confirm the timeline in your quote.

Yes. Licensed installation partners install your sign, with one Vision Graphics project lead managing the process. They handle the filing and installation, and our team prepares the drawings and coordinates the schedule, including after-hours work. We tell you who will be on site before installation day.

items.q: Can you replace an existing sign?
items.a_html: Yes. Removal is part of the install plan. A replacement is new work and may need its own permit, and the city's temporary protections for existing signs under Local Law 15 of 2026 do not cover a new sign. Send us a photo of your sign, and we will plan both steps.

items.q: What type of exterior sign is best for an NYC storefront?
items.a_html: Match the sign to who sees it. Channel letters suit storefronts open after dark, a blade sign catches pedestrians on busy blocks, and a fascia sign suits a clean facade. In landmark districts, non-lit or halo-lit lettering is often easier to approve.
